Neonates of the least weasel (Mustela nivalis) are among the smallest of all carnivores, with a wet weight at birth typically around 2.6 grams [Wwb = around 2.6 grams], though documented values in the literature range from 1.5 to 4.5 grams depending on litter size and maternal condition. This remarkably low birth mass reflects the species’ altricial developmental strategy, as newborns are blind, sparsely furred, and entirely dependent on maternal care. The subsequent growth trajectory is rapid, driven by a rich milk supply, and the young undergo a critical transition when they begin consuming solid prey, culminating in nutritional independence. At the point when maternal provisioning ceases, a process known as weaning, the offspring have typically attained a wet weight of approximately 43.5 grams [Wwx = approximately 43.5 grams]. This substantial increase from birth mass represents a more than sixteen-fold gain over a relatively short period, underscoring the high metabolic demands placed on the lactating female as she sustains a fast-growing litter. The weaning mass is a crucial milestone, marking the transition from suckling juvenile to independent, though still immature, predator.

The reproductive biology of the least weasel is tightly linked to its high metabolic rate and small body size. Under the typical core body temperature of 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C], which is characteristic of active, euthermic mustelids, the gestation period is surprisingly short, lasting only 36 days [tg = 36 days]. This abbreviated pregnancy is an adaptation that allows females to capitalize on brief pulses of prey abundance, particularly voles. Following parturition, the altricial neonates are housed in a nest where the mother provides warmth and milk. The time since birth at weaning is a mere 39 days [tx = 39 days], a developmental pace that is rapid even by mammalian standards at a temperature of 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C]. This accelerated life history is further reflected in a female producing around 1 pup per litter [N_R_i = around 1 pup per litter] and around 5 litters per year [F_R_i = around 5 litters per year], a combination that approaches the theoretical ceiling for a mammal of this size and is facilitated by their ability to breed year-round under favorable conditions.

Sexual maturation in the least weasel occurs remarkably early, a life-history trait that facilitates rapid population turnover. Under the sustained high metabolic temperatures typical of this species, namely 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C], both males and females attain puberty at 120 days since birth [tp = 120 days since birth]. This remarkably brief period between birth and the onset of reproductive viability means that females born early in the spring breeding season can themselves produce a litter before the summer ends. This capacity for early maturation is a key factor in the species’ ability to irrupt in numbers when prey is abundant. The physiological machinery underlying this early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis has been shown to be responsive to nutritional cues, with females achieving first ovulation shortly after reaching a threshold body mass. This early puberty, combined with a short gestation and rapid litter production, gives the least weasel one of the highest intrinsic rates of increase among terrestrial carnivores.

Adult body mass in the least weasel exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males considerably larger than females. Across their extensive Holarctic range, ultimate wet weight values vary substantially, but the species generally attains a maximum adult body mass of 177 grams [Wwi = 177 grams], with some records indicating that larger males can reach up to 208 grams [Wwi = up to 208 grams]. This size disparity is one of the most extreme among mammals and is believed to be driven by sexual selection, as larger males are better able to defend territories and access mates. Conversely, the smaller size of females is energetically advantageous for a species with such high reproductive output, as it reduces the absolute maintenance costs during lactation. The dimorphism is also associated with differences in home range size and hunting strategy, with males typically preying on larger rodent species than females. These morphological differences are established early in development and are maintained throughout the adult stage.

Longevity in the least weasel is relatively short, reflecting its fast-paced life history and high predation risk. Under the standard body temperature of 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 9.1 years [am = approximately 9.1 years], though survival to such an advanced age is exceedingly rare in wild populations where annual mortality rates are very high. Most individuals succumb to predation, starvation, or disease within the first year or two of life, with only a small fraction reaching reproductive senescence. This short lifespan is consistent with the species’ position as a small-bodied, high-metabolic-rate predator living in a variable environment. The energetic demands of maintaining a core temperature of 39.6 °C are substantial, and the costs of thermoregulation, especially during winter in northern latitudes, place significant constraints on energy budgets. Comparative studies with larger mustelids, such as the stoat, reveal that the least weasel trades off a long life for an early, intense reproductive effort, a classic example of a fast life-history strategy.
